name: Component Obsolescence

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors that change ownership are a longevity risk to designs: a company under financial pressure typically trims its product portfolio, cancelling individual chips that customers have already designed in.
claims.quote_verbatim: be concerned about the longevity of the parts, really, because if they start getting into trouble, then they might start cutting back on their number of products and their portfolio and stuff like that. And they cancel a chip you've designed in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Part selection can be overtaken by the component lifecycle itself: a month spent researching parts can end with some of the shortlisted devices already unavailable.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then by the time you finish that, they're all out of date and they can't get them anymore.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: A secondary market exists in which specialist manufacturers keep producing long-obsolete processors for military and aerospace programmes, at order quantities of a handful of units and prices on the order of $10,000 per chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: And there's a market for another 10 of them. So, they will actually produce them at, you know, $10,000 a chip or something like that.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Military Electronics and The Free Eagle (Freagle) Campaign

claims.claim_text: A sole-source part exposes a design to the vendor's internal restructuring: if the manufacturer stops producing that device, there is no drop-in alternative and the product cannot be built.
claims.quote_verbatim: If they turn around tomorrow because they're doing all these internal changes and they say, oh, we're not making that anymore. Yeah. You're up a creek without a paddle
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: A vendor end-of-life notice is one of the strongest triggers for reopening a finished design, because unlike cost or performance improvements it removes the option of leaving the design alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's a huge trigger if your vendor says you can't get any more
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: Redesign economics scale with annual volume: on a product selling 100 units a year carrying a $50 op amp, halving that part cost saves only about $2,500 a year, so an engineering change taking more than roughly 25 hours destroys the saving.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you do 50% better, you only save what? Two, $2,500 in a year. And if, if you're, if your change takes more than 25 hours
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: In large firms the obsolescence workflow is that a dedicated component obsolescence engineer identifies an unbuyable part and hands it to a design engineer, who then reworks the affected product.
claims.quote_verbatim: once the component obsolescence engineer came to me, I'd go and redesign based on that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A part can become unobtainable without ever being declared obsolete, when another buyer absorbs the available distributor stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not obsolete anymore, but some bastard's gone and sucked up all the stock
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Where an electronic module for a long-lived product is no longer manufactured, repair depends on a stockpiling aftermarket in which a large fraction of hoarded units have already failed from age and surviving units command high prices.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you'll have a failure rate of 80% just from age, but, you know, some of them will still work, and they'll charge a crap load of money
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Verbal longevity assurances given by a manufacturer at design-in time carry no weight years later, so a designer cannot defend a part choice on the basis that the vendor once said supply was secure.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't know it was going to go obsolete. Right, yeah. Well, you know, I asked them and five years ago they said, yeah. No problem.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Inability to source the original parts is one of the routine forcing functions behind a second generation of an open hardware project, independent of any desire for new features.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't get the same parts as you had before. So that is kind of moving on to the next generation
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Supply confidence is itself a design-in criterion: engineers select vendors partly on the expectation that the device will still exist long enough to avoid a forced redesign within two years of launch.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're trying to design in a product, you want to make sure that it's not going to be, you're not going to be redesigning it in two years
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Holding the bill of materials inside a distributor's own system lets a designer reorder in one step and see immediately which line items have gone obsolete or moved to a new version.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have my bomb in DigiKey.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: A common design-in rule is to avoid chips from startup vendors unless there is a compelling technical reason, because the probability of the company failing and the part disappearing within five years is high.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not going to go out and, uh, use a chip from a startup and unless I absolutely have to like the, you know, there's some massively compelling reason to do it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: A 'not recommended for new designs' status is effectively an early obsolescence warning, typically leaving two to five years of remaining availability before the part is withdrawn.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not recommended for new designs, but that's basically the death knell, right? That's like, okay, you get two or three or maybe five years, but you better watch your back
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: Obsolescence is costlier in modern systems than in discrete-logic eras: replacing a 74-series logic chip meant at worst a logic change, whereas a modern device carries firmware and application software whose changes propagate through the whole system.
claims.quote_verbatim: now there's so much software built on top of it, right? There's firmware and then there's software built on top of that. And it just propagates through the system.
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: Small-volume and one-off designers can sidestep obsolescence risk by selecting only parts currently in distributor stock and ordering components at the same time as the bare boards, an option unavailable to corporate programmes with long production lives.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can design around the parts you can actually get. So, you know, you don't have to worry about a component going obsolete in two years' time. You say, okay, what's in stock in Digi-Key?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Selecting a device because a development board was supplied by a vendor, rather than on supply grounds, repeatedly surfaces at production time as a twelve-week lead time or an obsolete part.
claims.quote_verbatim: their entire basis for choosing to use that chip, which when they then go to production and find, well, hang on it, oh, dear, it's on like 12-week lead time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers do not always offer a last-time buy; a part can simply disappear, leaving the buyer to purchase remaining world stock as the only mitigation.
claims.quote_verbatim: There was no last buy. It was just, you know, it was gone. Right? And, you know, we had to buy up the world stock.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: When an obsolete device defines a plug-in platform that installed modules depend on, substitution would break backwards compatibility, and the remaining route is to commission a manufacturer to copy the existing design and supply a compatible part.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to go find a manufacturer who was willing to copy that existing design and manufacture us a compatible one
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Analogue building-block parts used in instrumentation designs have gone out of production, including the XR2206 function-generator IC used in hobby and educational waveform generators.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like the waveform generator, the little that I used is gone now. The XR2206, I think it's, it's no longer made.
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Greg Charvat Returns With A Book! - Laboratory Literature Laureate

claims.claim_text: A small semiconductor vendor can only justify a sole-source design-in by offering a part so functionally unique that the customer's specification cannot be met any other way; without that differentiation the supply risk is not worth taking.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have to differentiate themselves by having a part that absolutely is so unique nobody else has that you've got no choice but to design that part in
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: Sorting candidate parts by distributor price can select a device whose low price reflects a distributor clearing stock after a line-card change, leaving the design with long lead times or a much higher price from other sources even though the manufacturer has not obsoleted the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: your low price might be because they're trying to get rid of stock at the distributor
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: Minimising the number of distinct line items in a bill of materials, rather than the total component count, is a design goal for hand-assembled products because each line item adds kitting and stocking labour.
claims.quote_verbatim: the number one thing that I wish I had done a better job of when I did the initial design is just using a fewer line items in the bomb
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: For a low-volume product that is selling steadily, the practical trigger for reopening the design is a component becoming unavailable rather than any accumulated wish list of improvements.
claims.quote_verbatim: the defining moment will be when a component is no longer available. That's when you say, oh, right now I've got to go work on this thing again.
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: Reimplementing a function from discrete parts when an integrated single-chip solution exists increases board area, cost and engineering time, and also raises obsolescence exposure because every additional component is another part that can be withdrawn.
claims.quote_verbatim: risk is a huge one as well, because then you have more components that can go obsolete, even if they are commoditized
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: Some turnkey assemblers maintain a house-parts library that is already loaded on their machines, offered below typical small-volume pricing with placement labour waived, with a guarantee of availability and a direct six-month notice before any house part is discontinued.
claims.quote_verbatim: we always guarantee those parts will be available. And if we're going to end the life in any of those, we give you a personal six month notice on that.
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: A conservative obsolescence policy at a large analogue vendor means parts are withdrawn only when production is physically impossible, such as a fab shutting down or the test equipment for the part no longer being usable, at which point a last-time buy is offered.
claims.quote_verbatim: TI's known as having a pretty good obsolescence policy, where we only obsolescence when we absolutely have to, right? You know, if the fab is shutting down or, you know, the test equipment can no longer be used
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: For very old parts the surviving documentation may exist only as scanned PDFs with no CAD source, so reproducing an evaluation board can require toner-transferring the layout image printed in the original application note.
claims.quote_verbatim: what you have to do is take the old eval application note, which is a scan copy
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Consolidation of legacy fabs drives batch obsolescence: a single last-time-buy announcement covered roughly a hundred devices built in one old National Semiconductor plant, including long-lived audio parts such as the LM386.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have, you know, probably 100 chips or so that are manufactured in some specific old national semiconductor plant somewhere.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers operate against an approved vendor list attached to the bill of materials, which authorises the factory to use named alternative manufacturers and component substitutions; that list is normally incomplete at production start and is filled in over the product's life.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a AVL approved vendor list and you've got a copy of the bomb. And basically you authorize the factory to use different manufacturers and different component substitutions.

claims.claim_text: Qualification effort for a substitute component scales with its function: a passive can be cleared by a paper qualification from the datasheet, whereas swapping something like a DC-DC converter requires a sample build and testing before approval.
claims.quote_verbatim: say you need to change DC to DC converters. You're probably not going to do that just by looking at a data sheet. You're actually going to want to build a sample build and do a bunch of testing.

claims.claim_text: Recording why each component value was chosen pays off during obsolescence work, because the substitution decision is usually made months or years later when the original constraints behind a value have been forgotten.
claims.quote_verbatim: why did I use a, you know, 4.7 microfarad cap and not a 10?

claims.claim_text: Engineering work does not stop when a product reaches volume production; sustaining effort continues for as long as the factory is building, because components go obsolete and materials become unavailable across the product's life.
claims.quote_verbatim: components go obsolete, stuff becomes unavailable, and you've got to continually support that

claims.claim_text: At companies whose boards carry hundreds to over a thousand components, monitoring component availability is a standing full-time role, because a manufacturing business earns nothing during any period it cannot build product.
claims.quote_verbatim: At some big companies, that's a real job.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mark Morin of Nufern

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding and product-launch platforms that manage supply chain for hardware creators typically handle only the cash-flow side, placing and paying purchase orders, rather than performing part substitutions as components go obsolete.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's mostly a cashflow, right? It's like, yes, we ordered another batch of 500 from seed or from whoever else.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Cheap application-specific chips sold through the Shenzhen market carry no availability guarantee, making them unsuitable for a commercial product with a multi-year service life unless supply is secured in advance.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're designing a commercial product that might have, you know, a five year, uh, product lifespan or something like that, you've got to be real careful buying these chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: One recommended hedge for a cheap but uncertain part is a lifetime buy sized far above forecast demand, on the order of fifty times the expected build quantity, with the inventory cost absorbed into the product's cost structure.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you find a chip you like and you think you might sell a thousand widgets, buy 50,000 parts or something like that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: There is no consolidated catalogue or datasheet repository for the custom ASICs sold in the Shenzhen markets, so parts that would be useful in a design are effectively invisible to engineers working from Western distributor catalogues.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no real repository of what's available in the Shenzhen markets
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A highly differentiated single-source analogue part can become a product-stopping liability when its lead time stretches, since no compatible alternative exists and replicating the function may take a dozen discrete devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: you design it in, you get all excited, and then you can't bloody buy the thing. That'll be a 40-week lead time, sir.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Programmes with a contractually mandated ten to twenty year service life bar designers from specifying parts whose vendors may discontinue them or go out of business, regardless of technical merit.
claims.quote_verbatim: Where they had to have by contract, like a 10, 20 year service life. Right. We, I would not, as a designer, I was not allowed to use a chip like this.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Silent specification changes between datasheet revisions are a recognised hazard, with vendors treating the errata and the revision letter as sufficient notice to the customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: You should have checked the errata. It changed from data sheet, rev J to K.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Distributor notification services cover obsolescence and discontinuation but not errata or specification changes, so datasheet revisions must be tracked by some other means.
claims.quote_verbatim: But that's for like obsolescence, not for errata.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Alongside obsolescence, high-volume manufacturing exposes component variation as a sustaining problem: incoming parts arrive bad, devices drift across their specified ranges, and multiple devices in one package that usually match are not guaranteed to.
claims.quote_verbatim: You see components come in and they're bad. You see components varying over their ranges. You see things like multiple devices in one package that usually behave the same, but then they're not guaranteed to.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: A last-time-buy announcement is not always final: a sufficiently large order can cause a manufacturer to reverse the decision and keep the line stocked, which makes end-of-life dates an unreliable planning input in both directions.
claims.quote_verbatim: A chip company's gone, last buys on this chip. Yeah. You know, we're shutting this down and then all of a sudden they get an order for 10 million chips. Right, right. And it's back in business.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because any production line can be shut down, the standard mitigations taught to designers are to prefer high-demand parts, keep firmware portable so a processor change is survivable, and document the design thoroughly.
claims.quote_verbatim: make your code portable. That's a good way to, as much as you can, right? Document your projects as much as you can.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Building a product around a commercial single-board computer transfers the whole business's continuity risk to another organisation's decision to keep manufacturing that board.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're totally reliant upon the continued manufacturer of that board
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Long-lived products often defer any refresh until the processor becomes unbuyable, at which point the end-of-life notice turns a deferred plan into an emergency.
claims.quote_verbatim: Usually people are like, oh, we'll be fine. We'll be fine. They're like, oh, crap, we can't buy the processor anymore
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Periodically re-quoting the whole bill of materials, on the order of every couple of months, is a practical way to detect parts that can no longer be bought before a build depends on them.
claims.quote_verbatim: run your bomb every couple months make sure they can actually buy the parts
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor mergers are treated as a leading indicator of obsolescence notices on the combined portfolio, prompting closer watch on affected parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: the hairs on the back of my neck kind of stand up when i hear about mergers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Specifying an obscure variant, such as an unusual package or the fastest speed grade with only a handful of customers, carries a double penalty: the variant is the first candidate for withdrawal, and during allocation its buyers sit at the back of the queue with no distributor stock to buy through.
claims.quote_verbatim: it might go obsolete you know because they might figure out that oh well now instead of five customers there's four customers

claims.claim_text: Large passive packages persist despite mobile-driven miniaturisation because voltage and creepage requirements cannot be met in the smallest case sizes; a mains-rated capacitor cannot be had in an 0201 package.
claims.quote_verbatim: Good luck getting a mains-rated cap in a bloody 0201 size package, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Obsolescence decisions at passive manufacturers are made by category economics rather than per-part: projected volume across an entire package and value category is assessed, and the whole category can be withdrawn together.
claims.quote_verbatim: when companies decide to make something obsolete, usually it's based on, like, okay, well, we ran the numbers and the, you know, the projection of all of the part, all of the 1206 parts in this category don't make sense
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Shifting an entire product to smaller passive case sizes purely to hedge against shortages is a poor trade, because it changes the assembly process technology, lowers yield and may force a change of assembly supplier; package choice should follow the product's own process requirements.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've just changed the whole assembly process technology, right? Yeah, I mean, you're going to have lower yield

claims.claim_text: Offloading a function to an external dedicated driver chip can be cheaper than moving up to a larger microcontroller in the same family, but it adds a bill-of-materials line item and therefore one more independent obsolescence and supply exposure.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a trade-off but then you've got another bomb item right and then you've got another thing that could go obsolete
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Within a microcontroller family, higher pin counts are only available in larger packages that also carry more memory and a larger die, so a design needing pins alone can end up paying roughly three times the cost for memory it does not use.
claims.quote_verbatim: the larger package comes with bigger memory right it comes with 128k of sram instead of 16k and you're paying for the bigger die
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Shortages of commodity passives leave engineering room to manoeuvre, since values can be substituted or in some cases components depopulated, whereas the loss of a unique controller chip has no equivalent workaround.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got a capacitor shortage okay you might be able to do some things substitute some stuff you might even be able to leave a few caps out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Obsolescence discovered after certification is far more expensive than obsolescence found during development, because a substitution can invalidate existing regulatory compliance such as FCC approval in addition to stranding fabricated boards and partly populated assemblies.
claims.quote_verbatim: what if you already got compliance right what if you already got yes right fcc compliance on something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Supply of a single-source part can be lost without any commercial decision, through the destruction or shutdown of the sole fab producing it, as happened to hard-drive production affected by flooding and earthquakes in Asia.
claims.quote_verbatim: or fabs burnt down that was the only place they made it right
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Where only one off-the-shelf power supply meets a product's requirements, the design is locked to a single vendor; specifying a custom magnetic component instead restores portability because the design files can be taken to any transformer manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: at least we can take our design files to any custom transformer manufacturer and get it made
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Obsolescence work is a recurring source of engagements for electronics consultants, arriving through contract manufacturers and distributor field application engineers whose clients need an unbuyable part designed out.
claims.quote_verbatim: their clients are having boards built there and something goes wrong or part goes obsolete. And they, I've gotten references to, you know, fix those for their clients.
claims.speaker: Eric Thompson

claims.claim_text: Management approval for a disruptive engineering change is far easier to obtain when framed as a supply deadline, with a named obsolete part and a stated number of months of remaining inventory, than as an argument from technical merit.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like part X is obsolete. We cannot buy it anymore. We have one year of parts left. We must switch in that time.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Components aimed at certified high-volume systems face a two to three year lag between launch and integration, because an integrator will not requalify a working certified system to save a few hundred dollars on a component; obsolescence cycles therefore overlap the design-in cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's definitely two or three years between a product being launched, uh, by me and it being integrated in a high volume production system
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: Manufacturer longevity guarantees are revised in practice; one documented response to a production line going down, which pushed lead time from two weeks to thirty, was for a customer to buy the entire world supply of the component.
claims.quote_verbatim: bought up the world supply of a particular component because that production line went down and it was, you know, the lead time went from two week to, you know, 30 week
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: On the electrical side of design for manufacture, sourcing questions such as whether a part can be obtained and whether it is heading for obsolescence trip up more projects than layout rule violations or pick-and-place capability limits.
claims.quote_verbatim: can I get this part? Is it going to go obsolete? Those kinds of things have seemed to be more of a, more of a pitfall on the electrical side

claims.claim_text: A bill-of-materials health risk assessment screens every line item against component databases and flags parts that are not recommended for new designs, scheduled for end of life, single-sourced, or carrying long lead times, so those decisions can be corrected before layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can look at any component and be like, Hey, you know, that one's not recommended for new designs, or that's going to be end of life, or this is available only from one supplier, uh, or it's got a really long lead time.
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Lead time on ordinary commodity parts can dominate a schedule: multi-layer ceramic capacitors reached roughly 72-week lead times, long enough to make a milestone unachievable if the exposure is discovered only after design-in.
claims.quote_verbatim: multi-layer ceramic capacitors for whatever reason had like a 72 week lead time. And if you didn't realize this and designed it into your product and are trying to hit a certain milestone that could be devastating.
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Under stringent regulatory regimes such as FDA oversight, medical device designs are deliberately frozen and changed only when a change is forced, which turns most ongoing engineering into obsolescence maintenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: we figure out when we have to change things and then we change things, but otherwise we don't change anything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Qualifying a replacement for a single obsolete component in a regulated product can absorb around six months of engineering effort, even for a part as simple as a transistor.
claims.quote_verbatim: This part's gone obsolete. Oh, let's spend the six months sourcing this new transistor.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Long-term purchase contracts do not guarantee supply: a memory device specified in a mid-2000s medical design became unavailable in the marketplace despite contracts being in place, leaving replacement as the only option.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have contracts in place to buy these parts, but it's just like some of them just aren't in the marketplace anymore. And so at that point you just have to replace it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A design left unmaintained for a decade accumulates a large backlog of obsolescence notices, so the absence of sustaining engineering is itself a source of technical debt on long-lived products.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have no one actually like maintaining it for 12 years, it's like, oh man, you think about the obsolete components
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Technically capable devices with small installed bases are discontinued regardless of merit, as with the Intel 196 microcontroller, leaving any surviving design that used it without a supply route.
claims.quote_verbatim: The 196 from Intel, the great little part, but practically no one used it and it's completely obsolete.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Under a fixed-quantity supply contract, buying the full chip quantity up front at contract signature removes obsolescence risk entirely for that programme, since the parts needed for every unit are already in inventory.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're contracted to produce 10,000 of these widgets. You buy 10,000 of the chips and you're sweet.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The escalation ladder for handling an obsolete component runs from dropping in a pin-compatible part and recompiling, through relaying out the board, to fitting a mod board such as a small flex PCB when existing built units must be modified without touching the original layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: worst case you would have to relay out your board. Um, you know, if you didn't want to touch the board, you wanted to modify existing products, you would do a mod board.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Free and unrestricted sampling by a manufacturer is not evidence that a part can be bought in production quantities; Maxim sampled generously while its chips ran to roughly 40-week lead times.
claims.quote_verbatim: you couldn't get them because the chips were like 40 weeks lead time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In product lifecycle management systems, obsoleting a component means creating a replacement item, revising the drawing that calls it out, and rolling that revision up through every assembly and higher-level drawing that contains it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you basically rev the drawing and then it just rolls all the way up the assembly
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Guaranteeing a multi-year supply commitment requires an owner inside the company, ideally multiple qualified vendors for every part on the board, and an automated tie-in to vendor end-of-life notification systems so that a last-time buy can be placed in time.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to tie into the vendors systems so that you automatically get notified if there's an end of life notice. Yeah. Right. So then you can do a last buy.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A published multi-year availability promise, such as an eight-year lifetime on a compute module, converts every end-of-life notice into a financial obligation: if no equivalent part can be engineered in, the vendor must fund an eight-year buy of the discontinued device.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they can't engineer an equivalent, find an equivalent, they have to buy an eight year supply of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: During a shortage the calculus shifts because the cost of waiting for an unavailable part exceeds the cost of revising the design, which pushes teams to redesign onto whatever functionally adequate part can actually be bought.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of waiting is much, much higher than the cost of revising
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A product change notification, or PCN, is the formal vendor mechanism announcing a change or discontinuation of a part; major distributors forward PCNs and last-buy notices to customers who previously purchased the part, effectively acting as an obsolescence monitoring service.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're buying these parts from a good supplier like Mouser or DigiKey, they actually will, if you bought these parts before, I think they will forward you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Within a microcontroller family a single character of the part number can halve memory and peripheral count and change package, so the nearest available family member may demand a layout change, a firmware rewrite and a revised system architecture rather than a simple substitution.
